question: A marketing coordinator asked Claude to "write an email about our new feature" and received a generic announcement that could describe almost any product. Which two changes to the prompt would most improve the next draft? Select two.
options: A) Send the same request a second time in capitals so the requirements are harder to miss.
B) Say who will receive the email and what they should do after reading it.
C) Paste in the real release notes rather than describing the feature in a single line.
D) Ask for a much longer draft, on the view that a longer email carries more useful detail.
E) Add a sentence asking Claude to write in a warm voice that readers will genuinely enjoy.
correct_answers: B) Say who will receive the email and what they should do after reading it.
C) Paste in the real release notes rather than describing the feature in a single line.
explanations: Repeating an identical prompt with added emphasis is the classic non-fix. Nothing new has been communicated, so there is no reason for the output to improve.

Correct. Telling Claude who will receive the email and what they should do afterwards defines what the email is for, without assuming anything about who those readers are. This is a separate fix from supplying facts: it constrains framing, emphasis and the call to action.
Correct. A generic draft is usually a symptom of missing source material. Pasting the real release notes gives Claude the specifics it otherwise has to invent or gloss over.
Length is not the problem. Asking for more words on an under-specified brief produces a longer generic email, and often padding rather than substance.
Style adjectives such as "warm" and "enjoyable" do not supply any of the missing product facts, so the draft stays generic and simply changes register.
